If unable to confirm submandibular sialolithiasis by examination, start with plain films or ultrasound (US) before moving to CT. C

background.definition: Sialolithiasis is the presence of calculi in the salivary glands or ducts. In order to be symptomatic, calculi must cause either partial or complete obstruction of the gland.

list.listitem: Twenty seven to 59 new cases per 1,000,000 persons per year. Only 3% of all cases involve children.
More common in men and in adults between the ages of 30 and 60 years.

Exact cause is unknown; appears to occur in the setting of chronic decreased flow within the salivary gland resulting in an accumulation of microscopic stones producing atrophic foci. Microbes may ascend the salivary duct, proliferate within these foci, and lead to additional stagnation and precipitation of calcium to form stones.
Exact mechanism is unknown; may be caused by presence of an organic nidus followed by deposition of other substances with progressive growth.
Most cases of sialolithiasis involve a single calculus and occur much more frequently in the submandibular gland (about 80%).
For patients with recurrent unilateral salivary gland pain and/or swelling, inspect the intraoral salivary duct openings and bimanually examine the involved gland as this may confirm the diagnosis. C
In patients with apparent submandibular gland involvement without a palpable or visible stone, plain radiographs, US, and CT may be useful. C
In patients with apparent parotid gland involvement without a palpable or visible stone, US and CT are most helpful for establishing the diagnosis. C
Referral for sialendoscopy (e.g. salivary gland endoscopy) may be required for patients in whom clinical evaluation and radiographic imaging are unsuccessful in confirming the diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Unilateral or bilateral parotids more often affected; fever, malaise, and myalgias
Parotid most commonly involved. Systemically ill. Very firm and tender gland
More likely in sublingual glands. Firm, fixed, often painless. Enlarging mass
Painless bilateral enlargement of parotids with diabetes, anorexia, or alcoholism

list.listitem: Sialolithiasis should be suspected in patients presenting with recurrent pain and/or swelling in a salivary gland associated with eating.
Examination including inspection of the intraoral duct openings and bimanual palpation of the gland can demonstrate a calculus.
Submandibular glands are far more commonly affected followed by the parotid glands; rarely seen in sublingual glands. The vast majority of cases are unilateral.

Although most submandibular calculi are radiopaque, the usefulness of plain radiographs is limited because of its relative insensitivity to small calculi and intraglandular stones. In addition, many parotid stones are likely to be radiolucent.

If using high-resolution noncontrast CT to assist in diagnosis, use fine (1 mm) cuts to prevent missing smaller stones. Although ultrasound (US) is operator dependent, it can detect more than 90% of stones at least 2 mm in diameter. Use of oral ascorbic acid may enhance visualization of the duct on US.
A meta-analysis found that ultrasound was 89% sensitive and 96% specific for diagnosis of sialolithiasis in submandibular or parotid glands and the associated ducts.

A retrospective study using sialendoscopy as the reference standard concluded that CT was 98% sensitive and 88% specific, although of course CT is associated with a significant radiation dose to the head and neck.
In cases where the etiology of salivary gland swelling remains uncertain despite initial evaluation including either US or CT, sialendoscopy is often successful in identifying pathologic findings.

For most patients, initially try a period of conservative management including hydration, local heat, gland massage, sialogogues, and analgesia. C
Patients with refractory or recurrent symptoms should be referred to an otorhinolaryngologist for further evaluation and management including consideration of sialoendoscopy. C
An initial trial of conservative therapy including hydration, local heat, and gland massage in hopes of promoting spontaneous passage of occlusive calculi is a reasonable option in most patients.
Sialogogues such as lemon drops can be useful to encourage salivary flow to help flush out distal stones.
NSAIDs can be helpful for analgesia as well as to decrease inflammation in the affected gland.
Antibiotics such as dicloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or clindamycin in usual doses for 10 to 14 days may be necessary if a concomitant acute bacterial sialadenitis is suspected.
Avoiding medications that may decrease salivary flow such as anticholinergic agents can also be helpful.
Multiple surgical approaches have been described and are variably indicated depending on the location of the obstructing stone(s).
Mechanical dilation of the duct orifice may allow passage of stones lodged in the distal ductal system.
Incisional transoral removal of stones is a safe and effective technique when stones are located in the distal portions of the salivary ducts.

Sialendoscopy can be useful for both diagnosis and removal of salivary gland stones, especially smaller stones in the ductal system. In 1 case series, authors reported a high rate of gland preservation using interventional sialoendoscopy for large stones (mean size 19 mm) in a hilar glandular location. A 2024 systematic review including 91 studies found sialendoscopy to be both safe and effective for diagnosis and treatment of obstructive salivary gland disease.
Avoiding complete removal of the affected gland is generally preferred in order to avoid complications such as xerostomia (a lack of saliva in the mouth) and intraoperative nerve injury.
Extracorporeal and intraductal lithotripsy are reasonably effective and minimally invasive treatment modalities in both submandibular and parotid disease.
Consider referral to an otorhinolaryngologist in patients with persistent or severe symptoms not responding to conservative management.
Patients with concerning symptoms for salivary gland tumors should also be referred for further evaluation including possible fine needle aspiration.

In a 5-center observational study of 4691 patients with salivary calculi treated with lithotripsy, endoscopy, basket retrieval, and/or surgery, stones were successfully removed in 80.5% and only 2.9% required salivary gland removal for treatment failure.

In another observational study with 42-month follow-up after intraoral removal of calculi, 101/118 (85.6%) remained asymptomatic, 14.4% had modest obstructive or infective symptoms, 3.4% suffered recurrent stones, and in 1 patient had persistent symptoms requiring salivary gland removal.
Children tend to present with a shorter duration of symptoms than adults.
Calculi tend to be smaller and more distally located thus increasing the importance of careful bimanual palpation of the oral cavity for diagnosis.
Optimal treatment strategy in children is similar to that in adults with preference for gland-saving approaches.
As systematic review of case series of children managed endoscopically for sialolithiasis found that the procedure was 95% effective in 133 reported cases, with a 2.8% rate of complications.
A systematic review of case series found that 85% of stones in children are submandibular, with a mean diameter of 7.7 mm.
